requirements: Reproduce the empirical study and the AlignGuard proof-of-concept testing tool for detecting correctness bugs in torch.compile.

sub_tasks.requirements: Set up the PyTorch environment, torch.compile versions (2.0-2.7), hardware (CPU + GPU), and dependencies required to reproduce the study and run all baseline techniques and AlignGuard.
Provision the hardware infrastructure matching the paper's experimental environment for running baseline testing techniques and AlignGuard.
Code has been implemented to verify the execution environment provides a 32-core (or greater) CPU server as described in Section 4.3.
Code has been implemented to verify access to NVIDIA GPUs (specifically three RTX 3090Ti GPUs as used in the paper, or equivalent CUDA-capable GPUs) for running GPU-backed torch.compile tests.

Code has been implemented to detect and select the appropriate device (CPU vs. CUDA GPU) at test dispatch time so that both CPU-backend and GPU-backend torch.compile bugs in the 77-bug benchmark can be reproduced.
Install and manage the range of PyTorch (torch.compile) versions required to reproduce all correctness bugs and evaluate testing techniques.

Code has been implemented to install all released PyTorch minor versions from 2.0 through 2.7 (inclusive), each in an isolated environment (e.g., separate conda/venv), covering the affected versions for all 77 benchmark bugs.

Code has been implemented to switch between buggy version V_B and fixed version V_F of torch.compile for each benchmark bug, so the detection criterion (test fails on V_B, passes on V_F) can be evaluated automatically.
Code has been implemented to record and log the exact torch, torch.compile, and CUDA versions used when executing each test case, so results are attributable to specific version pairs.
Install backend toolchains and low-level dependencies invoked by torch.compile during code generation and execution.

Code has been implemented to install a compatible GCC/Clang C++ toolchain used as the CPU backend of torch.compile, matching the compiler flags relevant to configuration bugs (e.g., -funsafe-math-optimizations).
Code has been implemented to install the Triton compiler versions bundled with (or required by) each PyTorch 2.0-2.7 release for GPU code generation.
Code has been implemented to install matching CUDA toolkit and cuDNN versions compatible with the installed PyTorch versions and the RTX 3090Ti (Ampere, sm_86) GPUs.
Install dependencies for the five baseline DL compiler testing techniques and for AlignGuard so all can be executed in the same infrastructure.

Code has been implemented to install Python dependencies for NNSmith, NeuRI, Opera, WhiteFox, and DeepConstr (each in its own isolated environment if version conflicts arise) with the pt2/torchcomp backend enabled.

Code has been implemented to install an LLM client library and configure API access (or a local model server) so that WhiteFox, DeepConstr, and AlignGuard's LLM-based test mutation can invoke an LLM at runtime.
Provide a reproducible, deterministic test-execution harness that isolates each test case's execution environment.
Code has been implemented to run each bug-reproducing test case in an isolated subprocess so that torch.compile crashes, non-determinism, or state leakage do not contaminate other tests.

Code has been implemented to seed Python, NumPy, and PyTorch RNGs and to clear torch.compile caches (e.g., torch._dynamo.reset()) between test executions to ensure reproducibility across the buggy and fixed version runs.
Code has been implemented to enforce a per-test timeout and resource limit so that hangs during torch.compile fuzzing do not stall the overall evaluation pipeline.
Reproduce the systematic collection and multi-stage filtering of 116 confirmed torch.compile correctness bugs from the PyTorch GitHub issue tracker.
Automated data collection from PyTorch's GitHub issue tracker for candidate torch.compile issues.
Code has been implemented that queries the PyTorch GitHub issue tracker (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues) for closed issues, restricted to closed status as described in Section 3.1.
Code has been implemented that performs a keyword-based search using the term 'torch.compile' to extract candidate issues.
Code has been implemented that restricts the collection period to April 19, 2023 through April 19, 2025 (inclusive of the cutoff date).

Code has been implemented that persists per-issue metadata needed for downstream filtering, including title, body/description, developer comments, labels (e.g., 'oncall: pt2'), close reason, and any linked pull requests or fix commits.
The initial pool of candidate issues gathered by the 'torch.compile' keyword search over the specified time range totals 2,542 issues, matching Table 1.
Multi-stage manual filtering pipeline that applies six exclusion criteria to identify confirmed correctness bugs.

Code/annotation infrastructure has been implemented that supports applying six sequential filtering steps as listed in Table 1 (non-bug issues, non-torch.compile issues, non-correctness bugs, unconfirmed by developers, duplicated, unclear root causes) and records per-step exclusion counts.

Step 1 filter is implemented to exclude non-bug issues (feature requests and general help requests), using absence of developer confirmation signals such as comments, linked PRs, or bug-specific labels.
Step 1 excludes exactly 581 issues, leaving 1,961 remaining, matching Table 1.

Step 2 filter is implemented to exclude issues not discussing a bug within torch.compile, using signals such as developer discussion, linked PRs modifying torch.compile code, or the 'oncall: pt2' label.
Step 2 excludes exactly 379 issues, leaving 1,582 remaining, matching Table 1.

Step 3 filter is implemented to include only issues whose symptom is a correctness bug (incorrect outputs of the compiled model), excluding exceptions, program crashes, memory leaks, and other non-correctness symptoms, based on issue description and developer discussion.
Step 3 excludes exactly 1,329 issues, leaving 253 remaining, matching Table 1.
Step 4 filter is implemented to exclude issues not confirmed by PyTorch developers (e.g., explicitly commented as expected behavior or closed without fix).
Step 4 excludes exactly 93 issues, leaving 160 remaining, matching Table 1.
Step 5 filter is implemented to exclude duplicated issues, either explicitly marked as duplicates by PyTorch developers or linked to a previously reported original issue without an additional fix.
Step 5 excludes exactly 34 issues, leaving 126 remaining, matching Table 1.
Step 6 filter is implemented to exclude issues unresolved, lacking clear root-cause description, or not linked to fixing commits in the issue discussion.
Step 6 excludes exactly 10 issues, leaving 116 remaining, matching Table 1.
Final curated correctness-bug dataset and its artifacts.
The final studied dataset contains exactly 116 confirmed torch.compile correctness bugs, matching Table 1 and Section 3.1.

Code has been implemented that exports the 116 final bugs together with fields required for downstream analysis: issue URL/ID, symptom (correctness), developer-confirmation evidence, linked fix commit/PR, and any reproducer code snippets extracted from the issue.
Reproduce the analysis of 296 high-priority PyTorch bug reports showing the distribution of faulty components and failure symptoms, matching the numerical findings in Section 2.2 and Figure 3.
Collect and prepare the dataset of 296 high-priority PyTorch bug reports from GitHub covering April 19, 2024 to April 19, 2025.
Code has been implemented to query the PyTorch GitHub issue tracker for issues labeled as high-priority within the date range April 19, 2024 to April 19, 2025.
Code has been implemented to filter the collected issues to retain exactly 296 high-priority bug reports matching the paper's dataset size.
Code has been implemented to persist each collected issue's metadata (title, body, labels, timestamps, comments) for downstream categorization by faulty component and failure symptom.

Categorize each of the 296 high-priority issues by its faulty component (e.g., Torch Compile, Eager Execution, Build, Configuration, Non-PyTorch Bug, Hardware Related, Tests, Parallel, CI, Feature Request, Others).
Code has been implemented to classify each of the 296 issues into one of the faulty component categories shown in Figure 3 (bottom/top-left) using labels and/or developer discussion.
Torch Compile accounts for 46.6% (138/296) of high-priority faulty components across the collected dataset, matching Section 2.2 and Figure 3.
Code has been implemented to aggregate the monthly counts of bug reports per faulty component across the 13 months (2024-04 through 2025-04) as visualized in the bottom bar chart of Figure 3.
Torch Compile is the most frequently reported faulty component in nearly every month between April 19, 2024 and April 19, 2025, matching the trend shown in the monthly bar chart of Figure 3.
Break down the 138 high-priority torch.compile issues by failure symptom (Crash, Correctness Bug, Memory leak, Performance, and other symptoms) as shown in the top-right pie of Figure 3.

Code has been implemented to classify each of the 138 torch.compile high-priority issues into one of the failure symptom categories (Crash, Correctness Bug, Memory leak, Performance, and other symptoms).
Correctness bugs account for 41.3% (57/138) of high-priority torch.compile issues, matching the value reported in Section 2.2 and Figure 3.
Program crashes account for 42.0% of high-priority torch.compile issues (0.7% higher than correctness bugs), matching the value in Figure 3 top-right.

Correctness bugs in torch.compile represent 19.2% of all 296 high-priority issues (57/296), matching the paper's abstract and introduction claim, and ranking as the second-most-common bug category behind program crashes (19.57%).
Compare the observed correctness bug ratio against the prior DL compiler bug study to reproduce the discrepancy discussed in Section 2.2.
Analysis reports that the 41.3% correctness bug ratio in torch.compile is substantially higher than the 26.3% (151/575) reported by the prior DL compiler bug study, matching Section 2.2.
Generate the Figure 3 visualizations (faulty component pie, symptom pie, and monthly stacked bar chart) reproducing the paper's presentation.
Code has been implemented to render the faulty-component distribution pie chart (bottom-left of Figure 3) with the categories and percentages listed in the paper.
Code has been implemented to render the failure-symptom distribution pie chart (top-right of Figure 3) for the 138 torch.compile high-priority issues.
Code has been implemented to render the monthly stacked bar chart of high-priority bug reports per faulty component across the 13-month window, as shown at the bottom of Figure 3.
Reproduce the categorization of the 116 correctness bugs in torch.compile into three main bug types and six subcategories with correct counts and percentages matching Figure 4 and Table 2.
Implement code artifacts that define the taxonomy structure of the 116 correctness bugs, including the three main bug types, six subcategories, and 'Others' category.
Code has been implemented that defines a taxonomy data structure listing the three main bug types: Graph-related Bugs, Operator-related Bugs, and Memory-related Bugs.

Code has been implemented that enumerates the six subcategories: Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs, Graph Caching Bugs, Operator Transformation Bugs, Low-Level Code Generation Bugs, In-Place Operation Handling Bugs, and Memory Layout Conflicts.
Code has been implemented that models the 'Others' category with its three sub-classes: Precision Bugs, Configuration Bugs, and External Library Bugs.
Code has been implemented that associates each subcategory with its dominant root cause and primary bug-triggering pattern as listed in Table 2.

Code has been implemented that flags the three high-frequency bug subcategories (marked with ✩ or ✩✩ in Table 2): Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs, Operator Transformation Bugs, Low-Level Code Generation Bugs, and In-Place Operation Handling Bugs.
Assign each of the 116 collected bugs to exactly one subcategory and produce aggregate counts per category and subcategory.
Code has been implemented that reads the 116-bug dataset and assigns each bug to exactly one of the six subcategories or the 'Others' bucket.
Code has been implemented that aggregates per-category counts and computes their percentage of the total 116 bugs, producing a Figure 4-style distribution.
The categorization pipeline verifies that the sum of bugs across all subcategories plus 'Others' equals exactly 116.
Reproduce the specific counts and percentages for main bug types matching Figure 4.
Reproduced count of Graph-related Bugs equals 23 (19.8% of 116), matching Figure 4.
Reproduced count of Operator-related Bugs equals 44 (37.9% of 116), matching Figure 4.
Reproduced count of Memory-related Bugs equals 39 (33.6% of 116), matching Figure 4.
Reproduced count of 'Others' bugs equals 10 (8.6% of 116), matching Figure 4.
Reproduce the specific counts and percentages for the six subcategories matching Figure 4.
Reproduced count of Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs equals 18 (15.5% of 116).
Reproduced count of Graph Caching Bugs equals 5 (4.3% of 116).
Reproduced count of Operator Transformation Bugs equals 21 (18.1% of 116).
Reproduced count of Low-Level Code Generation Bugs equals 23 (19.8% of 116).
Reproduced count of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs equals 25 (21.6% of 116), the most prevalent subcategory.
Reproduced count of Memory Layout Conflicts equals 14 (12.1% of 116).
Reproduce the counts for the 'Others' subcategories (Precision, Configuration, External Library bugs).
Reproduced count of Precision Bugs equals 3 out of 116.
Reproduced count of Configuration Bugs equals 5 out of 116.
Reproduced count of External Library Bugs equals 2 out of 116.
Generate the Figure 4 distribution visualization and Table 2 characterization from the categorized data.
Code has been implemented that produces a Figure 4-style pie/donut chart visualization showing both the three main bug type distribution and the six subcategory distribution with correct percentages.
Code has been implemented that renders a Table 2-equivalent table listing each subcategory with its description, dominant root cause, and primary bug-triggering pattern.

Reproduce the characterization of graph-related bugs (19.8% of 116 cases, 23 bugs total), including Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs (18 cases) and Graph Caching Bugs (5 cases), with their root causes, triggering patterns, case counts, and example bugs from Listings 1 and 2.
Reproduce the overall categorization and case counts of graph-related bugs.

Code has been implemented to load and label the 23 graph-related bugs from the curated dataset with their subcategory (Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs or Graph Caching Bugs) as annotated in Section 3.2.1.
The count of graph-related bugs equals 23 out of 116 total correctness bugs (19.8%), matching the reported distribution.
The count of Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs equals 18 out of 116 (15.5%) and Graph Caching Bugs equals 5 out of 116 (4.3%), matching Figure 4 and Section 3.2.1.
Reproduce the root cause classification for Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs (18 cases split into three root causes).

Code has been implemented that classifies each of the 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs into one of three root cause categories: Incomplete Symbolic Tracing for Custom Logic, Aggressive Optimization, or Lack of Fallback Handling for Unsupported APIs.
The count for Incomplete Symbolic Tracing for Custom Logic equals 9 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
The count for Aggressive Optimization equals 5 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
The count for Lack of Fallback Handling for Unsupported APIs equals 4 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
Reproduce the triggering pattern classification for Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs (18 cases across three patterns).
Code has been implemented that assigns each Graph Semantic Capturing Bug to one of three triggering patterns: Non-Computational Operations, Execution Context Mutation, or Corner Case Scenario.
The count for Non-Computational Operations pattern equals 9 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
The count for Execution Context Mutation pattern equals 5 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
The count for Corner Case Scenario pattern equals 4 out of 18 Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs.
Reproduce the illustrative Graph Semantic Capturing Bug example from Listing 1 (RewriteAddToMul TorchDispatchMode case).

Code has been implemented that reproduces Listing 1: defines a RewriteAddToMul(TorchDispatchMode) class whose __torch_dispatch__ replaces aten.add.Tensor with aten.mul.Tensor, defines model(x) returning x+x, and runs it under torch.compile with x=torch.tensor([3.0]) inside the dispatch mode.

On an affected torch.compile version, the compiled model output for the Listing 1 reproducer equals tensor([6.]) (buggy behavior where add is used instead of the dispatched mul), while eager or fixed execution yields tensor([9.]).
Reproduce the root cause characterization of Graph Caching Bugs.

Code has been implemented that documents/annotates all 5 Graph Caching Bugs with the root cause 'improper guard condition implementation that misses factors such as input properties (e.g., _max_seqlen, tensor shapes) or mutable internal model states'.

Code has been implemented that records the triggering pattern for Graph Caching Bugs as 'repeated execution of the compiled model with varying internal states or input properties', distinguishing it from single-compile differential testing pipelines.
Reproduce the illustrative Graph Caching Bug example from Listing 2 (self.value increment with cached graph).

Code has been implemented that reproduces Listing 2: a Model class with self.value initialized to -1, self.cache=torch.tensor([2,3,4,5,6,7]), a forward that increments self.value and returns self.cache[self.value], compiled with torch.compile and executed 6 times collecting outputs.

On an affected torch.compile version, the Listing 2 reproducer yields the buggy output sequence [2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5] (last two elements repeat 5 due to cached graph reuse), while the correct behavior yields [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
Produce the summary Table 2 row entries for graph-related bugs matching the paper's characterization.

Code has been implemented that emits a structured summary (e.g., CSV/JSON/table) with the two graph-related subcategories, each annotated with dominant root cause and primary bug-triggering pattern matching Table 2: (GSC -> 'Incomplete symbolic tracing for custom logic' / 'Models involving non-computational operations'; GCB -> 'Incorrect guard conditions for graph caching' / 'Repeated compilation with diverse internal model states').
The output labels Graph Semantic Capturing Bugs as a high-frequency subcategory (marked ✩) consistent with Table 2, and does not label Graph Caching Bugs as high-frequency.

Reproduce the characterization of operator-related bugs in torch.compile, covering Operator Transformation Bugs and Low-Level Code Generation Bugs. The characterization must include the total count (44/116, 37.9%), subcategory counts, root cause distributions, bug-triggering pattern distributions, and illustrative examples from Listings 3 and 4.
Reproduce the overall statistics for operator-related bugs, showing they are the most prevalent main bug type in the 116-bug dataset.

Code has been implemented that aggregates operator-related bugs (Operator Transformation Bugs + Low-Level Code Generation Bugs) from the annotated 116-bug dataset into a single main-category tally, producing a structured record with subcategory counts.
The measured total count of operator-related bugs equals 44/116 (37.9%), matching the paper's reported prevalence for this main bug type.
Characterize Operator Transformation Bugs (OTBs): incorrect transformation from high-level operators to low-level primitives, with a total count of 21/116 (18.1%).

Code has been implemented that classifies each operator-related bug as an Operator Transformation Bug or not, based on whether the bug arises during operator decomposition/fusion/lowering from high-level DL operators to low-level computational primitives.
The measured count of Operator Transformation Bugs equals 21/116 (18.1%), matching the paper's reported count for this subcategory.

Code has been implemented that assigns each Operator Transformation Bug to one of three root-cause labels: Computational Semantic Mismatch, Aggressive Optimization and Numerical Instability, or Transformation Incompatibility.

The measured Operator Transformation Bug root-cause distribution matches the paper: Computational Semantic Mismatch = 13/21, Aggressive Optimization and Numerical Instability = 6/21, Transformation Incompatibility = 2/21.

Code has been implemented that assigns each Operator Transformation Bug to one of three bug-triggering patterns: DL Operator with Non-default Parameters or Edge-Case Inputs, Optimization-Triggering DL Operator Sequence, or Configuration-dependent Scenario.

The measured Operator Transformation Bug triggering-pattern distribution matches the paper: DL Operator with Non-default Parameters or Edge-Case Inputs = 11/21 (with a 7/11 non-default-parameter vs 4/11 edge-case-input split), Optimization-Triggering DL Operator Sequence = 9/21, Configuration-dependent Scenario = 1/21.

A reproducible test case for the Listing 3 example (torch.diag_embed with input=x, dim1=-1, dim2=0, offset=1) has been implemented; under the buggy torch.compile version it produces a decomposed graph with aten.unsqueeze(cat, 6) and permute [6,0,1,2,3,4,5], while the fixed version produces aten.unsqueeze(cat, 0) and permute [0,1,2,3,4,5,6].
Characterize Low-Level Code Generation Bugs (LCGs): incorrect generation of low-level code (e.g., C++, Triton), with a total count of 23/116 (19.8%).

Code has been implemented that classifies each operator-related bug as a Low-Level Code Generation Bug or not, based on whether the bug is introduced during translation from Python-level operators into hardware-specific low-level code.
The measured count of Low-Level Code Generation Bugs equals 23/116 (19.8%), matching the paper's reported count for this subcategory.

Code has been implemented that assigns each Low-Level Code Generation Bug to one of three root-cause labels: Numerical Instability & Precision Mismatch, Lack of Boundary Scenario Handling, or Low-Level Language Incompatibility.

The measured Low-Level Code Generation Bug root-cause distribution matches the paper: Numerical Instability & Precision Mismatch = 13/23, Lack of Boundary Scenario Handling = 7/23, Low-Level Language Incompatibility = 3/23.

Code has been implemented that verifies every Low-Level Code Generation Bug in the dataset is triggered by compiling a single DL operator (rather than an operator combination), consistent with the paper's claim that these bugs are exclusively single-operator triggered.

Code has been implemented that assigns each Low-Level Code Generation Bug to one of two triggering patterns: Extreme Values for Numerical Sensitive Operators, or Single Primitive Operator with Unhandled Boundary Scenarios.

The measured Low-Level Code Generation Bug triggering-pattern distribution matches the paper: Extreme Values for Numerical Sensitive Operators = 13/23, Single Primitive Operator with Unhandled Boundary Scenarios = 10/23.

A reproducible test case for the Listing 4 example (torch.special.polygamma with n=1) has been implemented; the buggy generated C++ code branches only on x==0 (calc_digamma vs calc_polygamma), while the fixed version additionally handles x==1 via trigamma, and the buggy version exhibits larger numerical errors than eager execution.
Produce a consolidated summary table for operator-related bugs matching the layout of Table 2 rows for this category.

Code has been implemented that emits a Table 2-style row for each operator-related subcategory containing the subcategory name, description, dominant root cause, and primary bug-triggering pattern strings exactly matching the paper (e.g., OTB dominant root cause = 'Lack of boundary scenario handling logic'; LCG primary trigger = 'Extreme values for numerical sensitive operators').

Code has been implemented that flags Low-Level Code Generation Bugs as a high-frequency subcategory (matching the paper's ✩✩ marking) based on its subcategory share meeting the empirically-defined high-frequency threshold.

Reproduce the characterization of memory-related bugs (In-Place Operation Handling Bugs and Memory Layout Conflicts), including root causes, triggering patterns, and case counts as described in Section 3.2.3.
Reproduce the aggregate characterization of memory-related bugs as the second most prevalent bug type in the dataset.

Code has been implemented to classify each of the 116 collected correctness bugs into one of the two memory-related subcategories (In-Place Operation Handling Bugs or Memory Layout Conflicts) or mark them as non-memory-related.
The total count of memory-related bugs (In-Place Operation Handling Bugs plus Memory Layout Conflicts) matches the reported 39/116 (33.6%) of all collected correctness bugs.
Reproduce the characterization of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs (Bug 5), including their count, root causes, triggering patterns, and example.

Code has been implemented to define the In-Place Operation Handling Bugs subcategory as correctness bugs caused when torch.compile incorrectly optimizes or tracks in-place operations in user-defined models.
The total count of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs matches the reported 25/116 (21.6%), making it the most prevalent subcategory in the dataset.
Code has been implemented to categorize the root causes of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs into two subcategories: Incorrect Alias Tracking and Incorrect In-Place Operation Optimizations.
The count of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs attributed to Incorrect Alias Tracking matches the reported 17/25.
The count of In-Place Operation Handling Bugs attributed to Incorrect In-Place Operation Optimizations (e.g., functionalization errors) matches the reported 8/25.

Code has been implemented to document the bug-triggering pattern for In-Place Operation Handling Bugs as requiring in-place operations applied on tensor aliases (created by operations like view, expand) rather than plain in-place execution alone.

Code has been implemented to enumerate categories of aliasing-relationship creation patterns, including explicit tensor view operations (reshape, permute), slicing (basic/strided/masked indexing, offset slicing), and implicit aliasing (customized operators, nested mutable Python objects, tensor wrapping via torch.nn.Parameter).

Code has been implemented to enumerate categories of in-place operations that trigger this bug type, dominated by value assignment (indexed/masked updates, arithmetic operations like add_/clamp_/abs_) with additional shape/storage modifications (resize_, a.data = b) and implicit mutations (Triton tl.store, nonlocal variable assignment).

Code has been implemented to reproduce the Listing 5 example bug: a model where y = x.expand(2, *x.shape) followed by y[0, 0] = 5 produces an incorrect output tensor([5,2,4,6,8,10]) under torch.compile on the affected version, while the eager/fixed output is tensor([5,1,2,3,4,5]).
Reproduce the characterization of Memory Layout Conflicts (Bug 6), including their count, root causes, triggering patterns, and example.

Code has been implemented to define Memory Layout Conflicts as mismatches between tensor memory layouts (contiguous vs non-contiguous, channel-first vs channel-last) and the layout constraints of downstream operators during compilation.
The total count of Memory Layout Conflict bugs matches the reported 14/116 (12.1%) of the dataset.
Code has been implemented to categorize root causes of Memory Layout Conflicts into Incorrect Tracking of Layout Metadata and Missing Compatibility Checks for Layout Transformations.
The count of Memory Layout Conflicts attributed to Incorrect Tracking of Layout Metadata matches the reported 6/14.
The count of Memory Layout Conflicts attributed to Missing Compatibility Checks for Layout Transformations matches the reported 8/14.
Code has been implemented to categorize triggering patterns of Memory Layout Conflicts into Optimization-Driven Layout Transformations and Operator-Induced Layout Transformations.
The counts of Memory Layout Conflict triggering patterns match the reported 7/14 for Optimization-Driven Layout Transformations and 7/14 for Operator-Induced Layout Transformations.

Code has been implemented to reproduce the Listing 6 example bug: a model applying torch.argwhere then index_put where torch.compile generates buggy C++ code (loadu(in_ptr0 + int64_t(1L + x0), ...)) instead of the fixed version (loadu(in_ptr0 + int64_t(ks0 + x0), ...)), demonstrating incorrect memory access due to non-contiguous layout.
Produce the summary artifacts documenting the memory-related bug characterization as required for downstream use by other sections (e.g., AlignGuard, RQ2 analysis).

Code has been implemented to output a structured summary (e.g., JSON/CSV) mapping each memory-related bug in the dataset to its subcategory, root-cause label, and triggering-pattern label, matching the counts described in Section 3.2.3.

Code has been implemented to reproduce the Table 2 rows for memory-related bugs, listing In-Place Operation Handling Bugs (dominant root cause: Incorrect tracking of aliasing relationships; primary triggering pattern: in-place operations applied to tensor aliases or views) and Memory Layout Conflicts (dominant root cause: Missing layout compatibility checks; primary triggering pattern: operator sequences inducing memory layout transformation).

Set up and configure the five baseline DL compiler testing techniques (NNSmith, NeuRI, Opera, WhiteFox, DeepConstr) with the appropriate torch.compile backend configurations for evaluation on the correctness bug benchmark.

Code has been implemented to configure NeuRI with the backend set to 'torchcomp' so it fuzzes torch.compile.

A script has been implemented to integrate Opera's separate model structures and inputs into single executable test cases that invoke torch.compile and eager execution for differential comparison.
Set up WhiteFox as an LLM-based, optimization-aware fuzzer using its published torch.compile test cases.

Code has been implemented to execute WhiteFox's test cases against torch.compile without modifying their generation logic (no re-running of the LLM generation pipeline required for evaluation).
Set up DeepConstr as an LLM-based constraint-extraction fuzzer with the officially specified fuzzing command and configurations.
Code has been implemented to install and invoke DeepConstr using the officially provided fuzzing command from the DeepConstr artifact.
Code has been implemented to configure DeepConstr with the backend type, filter type, and 'mgen' configurations exactly aligned with the DeepConstr artifact defaults for torch.compile fuzzing.
Provide a unified execution harness for running all five baseline techniques across torch.compile versions and collecting bug-revealing tests.
Code has been implemented to run each of the five techniques across PyTorch released versions 2.0 through 2.7, covering the affected versions of all benchmark bugs.

Code has been implemented to run all baseline techniques on hardware including CPU and GPU (an environment with multiple GPUs such as three RTX 3090 Ti and a 32-core server, or equivalent) to match the paper's execution environment.

Code has been implemented so that every baseline technique, after execution, exports the set S_F[all] of all test cases it reports as bug-revealing (i.e., producing an output divergence between compiled and eager execution) in a uniform serialized format.
The five baseline techniques together comprise two grammar-based (NNSmith, NeuRI), one test-migration (Opera), and two LLM-based (WhiteFox, DeepConstr) approaches, matching Table 4 of the paper.
Construct the 77-bug reproducibility benchmark by filtering the 116 collected bugs based on reproducibility, patch availability, and hardware requirements, matching Table 5.
The benchmark construction pipeline is implemented with the correct sequential filtering criteria.
Code has been implemented that starts from the studied dataset of 116 confirmed correctness bugs (from Section 3) as the input pool for benchmark construction.

Code has been implemented that applies five sequential filtering steps in the order: (1) exclude bugs without reproducible code, (2) exclude non-torch.compile bugs, (3) exclude bugs without an identified patch, (4) exclude bugs not reproducible on a public release, (5) exclude bugs requiring non-CPU/GPU hardware.
Code has been implemented that records the count of excluded and remaining bugs at each filtering step, producing a table structurally equivalent to Table 5.
Each filtering criterion is implemented with the correct semantics matching the paper's description.
Code has been implemented that identifies and excludes bug issues lacking reproducible code snippets (minimal reproducible examples in the issue), based on issue content inspection.
Code has been implemented that excludes issues determined not to be torch.compile bugs (e.g., root cause outside torch.compile) based on developer discussion or linked patches.
Code has been implemented that excludes bugs where a fixing patch cannot be identified from the linked PRs or fix commits, since the detection criterion depends on patch availability.

Section 4.5.1: characterize why all graph-related bugs are missed.
The analysis reports that all 15 graph-related bugs in the benchmark (14 GSC + 1 GCB) are missed by every studied technique.
The analysis reports that 4 of the 15 missed graph-related bugs require dedicated (repeated-execution) testing pipelines rather than standard single-run differential testing.
The analysis reports that 6 of the missed graph-related bugs are associated with non-computational operators (e.g., control-flow APIs) that are not covered by baselines.
The analysis reports that 5 of the missed graph-related bugs arise from execution-context-mutation APIs (e.g., TorchDispatchMode) that baselines fail to include.
Section 4.5.2: characterize detected and missed operator-related bugs.

The analysis reports that 16 of the 33 operator-related bugs in the benchmark are detected collectively, composed of 9 OTBs and 8 LCGs (per paper's stated 9+8 detection counts, with 17 semantic-mismatch subset).
The analysis reports that 14 of the 17 detected operator-related bugs are single-operator semantic mismatch bugs (covering 6 OTBs and all 8 detected LCGs).
The analysis reports that the 3 detected optimization-related operator bugs are detected exclusively by WhiteFox, attributed to its white-box optimization-triggering pattern mining.

The analysis reports that 13 of the 16 missed operator-related bugs are single-operator semantic mismatch bugs whose target operators are covered by at least one baseline but require specific boundary/extreme input patterns.

The analysis reports that the remaining 3 missed operator-related bugs are optimization-related and require specific operator sequences (e.g., unsqueeze followed by mul-neg-div) not systematically generated by baselines.
Section 4.5.3: characterize detected and missed memory-related bugs.
The analysis reports that 6 of the 22 memory-related bugs in the benchmark are detected collectively, composed of 4 IPO bugs and 2 MLC bugs.

The analysis reports that both detected MLC bugs are identified by WhiteFox and are triggered by the conv2d operator implicitly mutating input tensor memory layout, with root cause 'Missing Compatibility Checks for Layout Transformations'.

The analysis reports that 3 of the 4 detected IPO bugs are detected by NeuRI and 1 by NNSmith, all triggered by in-place operations on tensor aliases/views created via basic operators (slicing, reshape, tile, zero-padding pad) with root cause 'Incorrect Alias Tracking'.
The analysis reports that the 16 missed memory-related bugs comprise 11 IPO bugs and 5 MLC bugs.

The analysis reports that for the missed IPO and MLC bugs, all in-place / layout-mutating operators (except one customized Triton operator each) are already covered by baselines, so misses are attributed to lack of complex alias/view usage patterns (e.g., unfold, nested list indexing, .data access) rather than operator coverage.
Section 4.5.4: characterize detected 'other' bugs.

The analysis reports that the studied techniques detect 3 other bugs, consisting of 1 precision bug and 2 configuration bugs, with the 2 configuration bugs sharing a GCC-flag-induced numerical instability root cause triggered by matmul and softmax on large-valued tensors.
